clue.text: Doctor to treat shingles?

parts.note: shingles are read as the wooden tiles on a roof, so the doctor sounds like one who mends buildings, while the real sense is a junior hospital doctor living in

explanation.surface: Someone asks which medic should be called for a painful bout of shingles.
explanation.walkthrough: Shingles looks like the viral rash, but it also means roof tiles, and a building is a house; the real term is a junior doctor resident in a hospital.
explanation.definitionFit: A resident junior hospital doctor is traditionally called by this title.

clue.text: I run Ted out — not given chance in Test

indicators.note: out signals that the letters are put out of their order and rearranged

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A cricket captain runs out a batsman called Ted, who never got a proper chance in the Test match.
explanation.walkthrough: 'out' rearranges IRUNTED. In the surface Test is a cricket Test match and running out is a dismissal.
explanation.definitionFit: Something never put to a trial has not been tested yet.

clue.text: Almost never lifted, like Wenceslas's snow

indicators.note: in a down clue lifting a word raises it upward, so it reads backwards
almost means the word is not quite complete, so its final letter is dropped

explanation.surface: Snow that hardly ever lifts, like the snow in the carol about Good King Wenceslas.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Almost' cuts NEVER to NEVE and 'lifted' turns it up to give the answer. The carol 'Good King Wenceslas' has snow lying 'deep and crisp and even'.
explanation.definitionFit: The carol describes the snow as deep, crisp and level all over.

clue.text: Good place for William as things turned out …

indicators.note: turned out signals the letters are turned around into a new arrangement

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: The battlefield proved a good spot for William, as events turned out.
explanation.walkthrough: 'turned out' rearranges ASTHINGS. William the Conqueror won the battle there in 1066, which the next clue continues.
explanation.definitionFit: William the Conqueror defeated Harold at this battle site in 1066, so it served him well.

clue.text: in south-east — 1066 typically — stayed, we hear

parts.note: SE is the compass abbreviation for south-east
1066 is a famous example of a historical date

explanation.surface: Continuing the previous clue: the battle in south-east England in 1066 is where things stayed put.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition plays on sound: 'stayed' is said like 'staid', which means calm and serious. Hastings is in south-east England, linking back to the previous clue.
explanation.definitionFit: Staid and calm, unexcitable behaviour are both close synonyms.

clue.text: He might support striker whilst helping others back at work

definitions.text: He might support striker whilst helping others back at work

parts.words: He might support striker whilst helping others back at work
parts.note: reads like a fellow worker backing a colleague on strike, but in football the striker is a forward and the backs are the defenders this player helps

explanation.surface: A trade unionist backs a colleague on strike while helping fellow workers return to work.
explanation.walkthrough: Striker suggests an industrial dispute; in football it is the attacking forward, and a back is a defender, so the clue describes a central defensive player.
explanation.definitionFit: This football position sits in the middle of the defence, among the backs, and feeds the forwards.

clue.text: Work on cartoon in main tea-break

indicators.note: break signals the letters are broken up and reassembled

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: An animator works on a cartoon during the main tea break.
explanation.walkthrough: 'break' rearranges MAINTEA.
explanation.definitionFit: To bring drawings to life as moving pictures is the key task in making a cartoon.

clue.text: eg runes, not delivered or claimed

definitions.meaning: runes are characters of an obsolete alphabet no longer in use
post office mail that could be neither delivered nor collected

explanation.definitionFit: Obsolete alphabet characters are lifeless writing symbols, and undeliverable mail ends in the post office department of that name.

clue.text: Turnover puddings can be strained

indicators.note: turning a word over makes it read in the opposite direction

parts.note: desserts are puddings, the sweet course

explanation.surface: Apple turnovers and other puddings can be put through a sieve.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Turnover' looks like a pastry but tells you to turn DESSERTS backwards.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone under strain and tension is anxious and overwrought.

clue.text: Ingenuous, dotty one in body of church

indicators.note: in places the one letter within the church word

parts.note: the nave is the main body of a church
I is the Roman numeral one, and here it carries the two dots of a diaeresis

explanation.surface: A simple, slightly crazy soul sits in the main part of the church.
explanation.walkthrough: 'dotty' looks like 'mad' but refers to the dots over the I in the French spelling with a diaeresis.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone ingenuous is innocent and unworldly, trusting without suspicion.

clue.text: Sward-swallowing?

parts.note: sward is grassy turf, so something that swallows grass is a plant-eating animal, punning on sword-swallowing

explanation.walkthrough: Sward, an old word for turf, sounds like the circus act of sword-swallowing.
explanation.definitionFit: A plant-eating animal grazes on grass and greenery.

clue.text: Long film of the "Pickwick Papers

indicators.note: of signals that the answer is taken out of the following words

explanation.surface: A lengthy screen adaptation of Dickens's The Pickwick Papers.
explanation.walkthrough: The letters run across 'thE PICkwick'; 'Papers' completes the book title in the surface.
explanation.definitionFit: A grand, lengthy film on a large scale is called by this term.

clue.text: Lantern hid secretly in remote, undeveloped area

indicators.note: secretly suggests the letters are disguised by being rearranged

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone hides a lantern secretly out in the wilds.
explanation.walkthrough: 'secretly' rearranges LANTERNHID.
explanation.definitionFit: The back country away from towns and coast is an undeveloped region.

clue.text: Ned Kelly was one painted on a roundabout

indicators.note: roundabout signals the letters go round and come out in another order

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A picture of the outlaw Ned Kelly is painted on a fairground roundabout.
explanation.walkthrough: 'roundabout' rearranges PAINTEDONA. Ned Kelly was a famous Australian bushranger, and Australia lies on the opposite side of the globe from Britain.
explanation.definitionFit: Ned Kelly came from Australia, at the far side of the world from Britain.

clue.text: Playful talk unsuitable for the elderly?. .

parts.note: bad means unsuitable or not fit
the elderly are people in old age, so this reads as in age

explanation.surface: Banter may be considered unfit for older people.
explanation.walkthrough: The clue reads 'bad in age' as unsuitable for the old; the question mark flags that reading.
explanation.definitionFit: Light, teasing conversation and banter is a playful kind of talk.

clue.text: … an old joke can mean symptom of chest trouble

definitions.meaning: a stock gag or trick that has been around a long time
a whistling breath sound caused by asthma or bronchitis

explanation.definitionFit: The word means both a hackneyed gag and the rasping breath of a wheezing chest.

clue.text: Covered with ash, perhaps -Flying Officer took a breather

parts.note: FO is the abbreviation for Flying Officer, an RAF rank
to take a breather is to have rested

explanation.surface: A Flying Officer pauses for a rest, covered in ash from a fire.
explanation.walkthrough: Ash looks like fire debris but is the tree; ash trees are an example of woodland cover.
explanation.definitionFit: Land covered with trees, such as ash, is wooded.

clue.text: Wild civets found in Isle of Wight once

indicators.note: wild suggests the letters run free and come out disordered

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Wild civets turned up on the Isle of Wight long ago.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Wild' rearranges CIVETS.
explanation.definitionFit: The Romans called the island off England's south coast by this Latin name.

clue.text: Turnover that must be quoted to hatter?

definitions.meaning: an overturning, as of a boat

definitions.text: that must be quoted to hatter?
definitions.meaning: a hatter needs the measurement of one's head to fit a hat

explanation.definitionFit: A boat overturning is a capsizing, and the head measurement given to a milliner is a hat fitting.

clue.text: China has solid fuel left in the main

parts.note: coal is a solid fuel
the main is the sea, and on a ship the left side is port

explanation.surface: China imports solid fuel and leaves it at sea.
explanation.walkthrough: 'China' looks like the country but is porcelain: Coalport is an English maker of fine china. 'The main' is an old word for the open sea.
explanation.definitionFit: Coalport is an English porcelain factory whose wares are a type of china.

clue.text: Art work on paper out east?

definitions.text: Art work on paper out east?

parts.words: Art work on paper out east?
parts.note: an art practised with paper folding, which comes from Japan in the Far East

explanation.surface: A drawing on paper made somewhere in the Orient.
explanation.walkthrough: Art work on paper suggests drawing or painting; it is the Japanese craft of folding paper into shapes.
explanation.definitionFit: This Japanese craft folds paper into figures without cutting.

clue.text: Subdued grumble as double grog-ration is knocked over

indicators.note: in a down clue knocking something over turns it upside down, reversing it
double means the piece is written twice

parts.note: grog is rum, the sailors' daily ration

explanation.surface: Sailors complain quietly when a double tot of rum is spilled.
explanation.walkthrough: 'double' gives RUMRUM and 'knocked over' turns it round.
explanation.definitionFit: A low complaint muttered under one's breath is a quiet grumble.

clue.text: Public Relations Officer, in straitened environment, had kids

indicators.note: in, with environment, places one piece inside the surroundings of another
environment names the surrounding piece that encloses the officer

parts.note: straitened circumstances are reduced ones
PRO is the abbreviation for Public Relations Officer

explanation.surface: A PR officer in hard-up circumstances has started a family.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in straitened environment' puts PRO inside REDUCED.
explanation.definitionFit: To have children is to bear offspring and breed.

clue.text: On this platform, one is sure to be late

definitions.text: On this platform, one is sure to be late

parts.words: On this platform, one is sure to be late
parts.note: late reads like a train running behind time, but it means deceased: everyone on earth is a mortal who will one day die

explanation.surface: A railway platform where your train is certain to be delayed.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Late' means dead, so 'one sure to be late' is one who dies, which every mortal does.
explanation.definitionFit: A mortal being who will eventually die is one destined to be the late so-and-so.

clue.text: Only half find out that is a record

indicators.note: only half means just the first half of the word is kept

parts.note: to discover is to find out

explanation.surface: A researcher finds out only half the story from a record.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Only half' keeps the first four of DISCOVER's eight letters.
explanation.definitionFit: A gramophone record is a flat circular platter.

clue.text: Make one have the smallest share of trust with Edgar initially

parts.note: a unit trust is divided into units, the smallest share you can hold

indicators.note: initially means take the first letter of the next word

explanation.surface: An investor with Edgar joins forces with the smallest stake in a trust.
explanation.walkthrough: A unit trust is a British pooled investment fund sold in units.
explanation.definitionFit: To join things into a single whole is to unify them.

clue.text: The calamity at sea, doing without tea -like the Flying Dutchman?

indicators.note: at sea means confused, so the letters are jumbled

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written, the letters removed

explanation.surface: A disaster at sea with no tea on board, like the legendary ghost ship.
explanation.walkthrough: 'at sea' rearranges THECALAMITY and 'doing without' removes the letters of TEA. The Flying Dutchman is a legendary phantom ship.
explanation.definitionFit: The Flying Dutchman is a legendary ghost ship, so it belongs to folklore.

clue.text: Is it effected when meeting déja-vu sufferers?

definitions.text: Is it effected when meeting déja-vu sufferers?

parts.words: Is it effected when meeting déja-vu sufferers?
parts.note: someone with deja vu feels they have met you before, so presenting you to them feels like a second presentation

explanation.surface: Someone wonders what happens when you are presented to people who feel they have seen it all before.
explanation.walkthrough: Deja vu is the feeling of having experienced something already, so being presented to such people feels like being presented again.
explanation.definitionFit: Presenting people to one another a second time is a repeated presentation.
